Buildings, Hospitals, Sanatoria, Soldiers' Homes, Vocational Training Centres, etc., $1,300,000.
['I move that item No. 29 be amended by striking out the words "So-\n\nlicitor at $4,000" and by reducing the total amount from $71,200 to $67,200.']

The expenditure under this head for 1918 amounted to $1,700,000 and this Estimate is $400,000 less. The expenditure covers hospitals for general purposes, sanatoria for the treating of tuberculosis, homes for incurables, and buildings for vocational training. The department is now erecting new buildings in almost all the provinces. There is one at Tranquille, British Columbia, where the department, in co-operation with the British Columbia Anti-tuberculosis Society is erecting an extension for the housing of 130 patients, together with dining room and kitchen accommodation. In Alberta the department with the co-operation of the provincial government is erecting a building to accommodate 175 beds for the treatment of tuberculosis.
What is the expenditure?

I can only give an estimate. It is- probably very near $300,000. In Manitoba the department is contributing towards the accommodation for the treatment of tuberculosis in the provincial sanatorium at Ninette. The Manitoba Anti-tuberculosis Society is setting aside sufficient accommodation for the exclusive use of this department. In most cases the department has made arrangements with the provincial governments or some recognized institution whereby the department provides for the extension of the existing institutions in order to care for the patients. As a result of experience', the department has reached the conclusion that that means in the long run a substantial saving to the Federal Government.
In Quebec, with the co-operation of the provincial government the department is erecting 200 beds for the treatment of tubercular patients at the Laurentian Sanatorium.
In New Brunswick, the department has recently assumed the administration of Jordan Memorial Sanatorium at River Glade, N.B., and is making provision for extra accommodation at this institution.
In Nova Scotia, through the co-operation of the Nova Scotia government, the department is completing certain buildings at the' Nova Scotia Sanatorium.
In Halifax, in order to provide for active treatment cases, the department, through

the Public Works Department, is erecting a 50-bed active treatment hospital.
In Prince Edward Island, the accommodation is being completed at Dalton Sanatorium, for the treatment of tuberculous patients.
Over and above the foregoing, the department, in operating the large number of institutions coming under its control, must of necessity provide funds for the maintenance and upkeep of various buildings. The members of the committee will see that we must meet the demands made upon this department to care for all returned soldiers suffering from tuberculosis. The cases that come under its charge are not those in which an immediate recovery is expected. They are discharged from the military forces as soon as this disease is diagnosed and are passed into the hands of this department. I am sure all will agree that the country should do everything in its power to provide the best possible treatment for ex-members of the forces who are suffering from tuberculosis. These expenditures are necessary in order to provide sanatoria where they can be treated. This is usually accomplished by an extension to an existing institution thus saving the cost of erecting a new building.

Has the dental corps
been transferred from the Militia department to this new department?
No.

I understand that a
decision had been arrived at some time ago.

The Militia department
has not transferred the Dental Corps to the Soldiers Civil Re-Establishment department. The Militia department is treating the returned soldiers who require dental treatment immediately upon discharge, but the Soldiers Civil Re-Establishment department must necessarily provide dental treatment for those who come under its charge and establish its own branch for this particular work.

In connection with 1he programme outlined by the minister, I think the department is taking the right line in co-operating with the provincial authorities, in using sanatoria and other hospital accommodation in the different provinces and assisting in putting up buildings that will toe of some value to the country after the work of reconstruction is completed. In my experience of the working of the Militia Department and the Military Hospitals Commission, prior to the Soldiers Civil Re-establishment Department being
established, there never has been a more wasteful expenditure of public money than that which took place as between these two departments. Buildings have been erected for hospital purposes of a semipermanent character which, now that the war is over, appear to toe absolutely useless and the money is thrown away. I do not know whether the minister of this new department intends to use these hospitals which have been built in almost every province in Canada. If nothing can be done to utilize these buildings on which millions of dollars have been expended, it will toe a great loss to the taxpayers of this country. I am pleased to learn that the department proposes to take over and assist existing institutions which, in any event, will toe of some value to the people after the war. I would suggest to the minister in charge of the department in this House that he bring to the attention of the responsible minister the fact that thousands of dollars have been wasted between the Militia Department and the old Military Hospitals Commission; whether through jealousy or lack of co-operation, I do not know. The fact remains that in every town in Canada almost the same condition has prevailed, money being wasted toy one department or another that might have been used to better advantage had there been proper co-operation between these two departments.
Is there any provision for hospital accommodation for invalided soldiers who never left Canada?
They stand on the same basis as those invalided from overseas.

I am glad to hear that because I have been fighting a case now for pretty nearly a year and a half. In 1916 we had a man in Swift Current, Mr. McIntosh by name, who enlisted in the 209th Battalion. He is a married man, 39 years of age, has a wife and five children and is a machinist by trade. He was.examined by the battalion medical officer and taken on the strength as medically fit. He went to Camp Hughes and put in the summer there. He broke down under the training and when the battalion left he remained in Camp Hughes, was discharged as medically unfit and went home. Since that day the city of Swift Current has kept him and his wife and family. The returned soldiers pay the rent of the house for the family, which amounts to $15 a month; the town of Swift Current pays $80 per month to keep the family, and it sent him to the Mayo hospital for

treatment. The hospital sent him back and said he had broken down under army training and probably would never be much better. I brought the matter to the attention of one department after another, and let me tell you they are past masters at passing the buck. They sent me from one department to another. They sent me to the Pension Department, and the Pension Department told me that there was no provision at all for a case of that kind, that it was a recurrence of a former disability. There ought to be responsibility somewhere, and somebody has to assume it. The Militia Department took that man on the strength as medically fit on their own doctor's certificate, and I am going to stay With the job until the thing is straightened out. Up to date the town of Swift- Current has paid $1,500 to maintain that family ever since the man was discharged, and I want to know -who is going to reimburse the town.
I can understand the action of the Pension Board in saying that it was a recurrence of a disability. What is the other department to which my hon. friend presented the case?

The Invalided Soldiers Commission, and then the Pension Board. The Pension Board said that they had no jurisdiction over the case at all, and that there was no provision to meet it. I do not know how it will end, but I am going to keep on pressing the case.

I should think it would be a case for consideration by the Soldiers Civil Re-Establishment Department. The deputy minister will look into the matter and take it up if my hon. friend will give him the facts. I think the Pension Board is correct in saying that it did not come properly before it.

I want to assure the minister that I have given them the facts more than once.
Major-General MEWBURN: Has he been discharged from the Canadian Expeditionary Force?
Yes, as medically unfit for military service. He was given his ticket, sent home, and that was the last of it.

The deputy minister will take the matter up and look into it. Jf the facts are as stated by my hon. friend, I should think that it was a case for treatment in one of the institutions of the department.

We have tried several times to get them to take him back and give him
[Mr. Argue.l
treatment, or put him under observation. I have done my best to see if something could not be done, but up to date I have not been able to get any action.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman give the name?
I will give you the name and all the particulars.
How many tubercular soldiers are at present in sanatoria throughout Canada, and how many beds are there for tubercular soldiers?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that question would be more in order under item 334.
Do I understand that the cost of dental services is provided for under this vote?

No, this relates only to buildings. I just want to make one observation to prevent a misunderstanding, with respect to the remarks of my hon. friend from Strat-hcona, and I do so because I think the Minister of Militia was not in the House when my hon. friend spoke. If either of the two departments had known that the war would come to an end when it did, much less accommodation might have served, and much less building would have been gone on with; -but as the situation looked last summer almost right up to October, until September, anyway-and I recall this- matter having been repeatedly presented to Council-owing to the severe casualties sustained in the August drive and the casualties which it was expected would be sustained during the year, it became necessary to evacuate as many hospital cases to Canada as possible. Men were coming back to Canada, and the complaint constantly -made to the Department of Militia and Defence was that there was not sufficient hospital accommodation for them in the principal military centres of Canada, and it was urged that additional accommodation be provided. The department, therefore, in their view of the case, were unable to turn over these institutions to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment because they were being used for men who came under the Department of Militia and Defence. Now that peace has come, just as soon as the Department of Militia and Defence is prepared to surrender one of these institutions it is being surrendered, if suitable, to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment for their work. I happen to have personal knowledge of quite a number of hospitals which have been turned over in that

way recently. 1 think that, in a measure, will explain what my hon. friend has re-. ferred to.

I give a clear case of lack of co-operation 'between the two departments in my own constituency. The Military Hospitals Commission rented from the Alberta College a building for, I think, $11,000 a year, on the understanding that the building was to be returned in the same condition in which it was received. Last year the Military Hospitals Commission expended something like $50,000 on this building for new plumbing, baths, and work of that kind. The equipment had all been put in, with the exception of the boilers required to make the baths available, when the armistice was signed. The result is that the entire expenditure is wasted; the equipment has never been used, and if the Commission turns the building over in the condition in which it was received it will have to take out every part of that equipment. Again, the city of Edmonton offered to the Militia Department the use of one of the best hospitals in Western Canada free of charge; it had all the necessary facilities and accommodation for 180 patients, but through lack of co-operation between Military District No. 13 and possibly the Military Hospitals Commission, this hospital was caring for only twenty or twenty-five patients instead of one hundred and eighty. What I am complaining of is the lack of co-operation between the two departments, which has resulted in an expenditure of money which can never be justified.
What is the policy of the department with regard to epileptics and tubercular cases? Is it still the policy to unload them on the civilian institutions, as was done a year ago?

I am not aware that that was the policy, and so I am advised by officers of the department. The policy is to take care of these men until they have recovered, and that is the object of these various institutions for which I am asking this vote.

My point is this: Instead of the 'Government taking care of these cases in their own institutions and with their own doctors, they were turned over to civilian institutions at a cost of so much per day or per month. Is that still the policy?

No. The policy is for the department itself to care for these patients
in these institutions for which we are asking this money.

I am very
pleased to hear that statement. I raised this question a year ago, but I did not get much consideration. I trust that more accommodation will be provided in the future than in the past. I have visited many of the civilian institutions from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and I did not find one where I thought the men were getting sufficient care and treatment. I am very glad to know there has been a change.

I am glad to say that
the results of the treatment have been very satisfactory. About seventy-five per cent of the men treated have been able to resume work in gainful occupations.

At what centres
is vocational training being given in connection with the hospitals, and is there any arrangement with the provinces to assist in providing buildings for this purpose? About what proportion of this vote of $1,300,000 will be devoted to vocational training?

There are some twelve
centres in which vocational training is being given at the present time-Montreal, Ottawa, Halifax, Kingston, Toronto, London, Winnipeg, Calgary, Guelph, Regina, Victoria and Fredericton. Besides the departmental training centres there are outside schools to which the pupils are sent. A number of men are also under training in industrial establishments under actual working conditions. In the Quebec district, last year there were 3 schools carried on by the department directly, and 4 this year; Nova Scotia, 2 last year, and 3 this year; Central Ontario, 3 last year, and 2 this year. Central Ontario, 8 last year, 8 this year; Western Ontario, 3 last year, 2 this year; Manitoba, 1 last year, 2 this year; Saskatchewan, 3 last year, 3 this year; Alberta, 3 last year, 2 this year; British Columbia, 3 last year, 5 this year; New Brunswick, 1 last year and 1 this year. The total number last year was 30, this year 32. The principal increase has not been in the schools under the direct charge of the department, but in other schools with which the department has made arrangements-institutions of the provinces, universities, and other schools. The total number of those last year was thirty-seven; this year one hundred and twenty-seven. So that the department has, during the year, been carrying out the policy of co-operating as far as practicable with the various provincial gov-

ernments and the educational organizations of the provinces in order to utilize those schools for vocational work as indicated by the increase and so reduce capital' expenditure.
One of the most important features of the retraining is in connection with the men working with independent firms. In fact, the war veterans have impressed very strongly upon the department that the men should have their practical .training by working under ordinary business conditions. The number of firms in which soldiers are engaged in that way has increased from fifty-seven in March, 1918, to nine hundred and ninety-three in 1919.
I notice you stated that Calgary had three schools last year and it now has two. Is one of those schools located in Edmonton?
There is one in each place.
Is any provision made for getting this vocational training at night, or is it all during the day?

The department has not made any provision for training at night. Soldiers who are taking this retraining are disabled, and night classes- would impair their physical well-being. As they receive pay and allowances when receiving retraining there is no hardship entailed.

The reason I ask the question is that I have been approached by a number of men who are in employment part of the day, and who would like to have the privilege of attending some classes at night in order to make themselves more proficient.

As I understand my hon. friend's question, he is referring, not to disabled men, but to soldiers who are physically fit and who would like to qualify themselves more effectively for their particular work.

Not exactly what you might call totally disabled. They are able to carry on, and they have employment which they are not exactly satisfied with, and -they would like to qualify themselves for something better.

The question my hon.
friend raises is one deserving careful consideration, and I will commend it to the officers of the department. So far the department only deals with disabled men, that is, men who are so disabled that they cannot carry on their pre-war occupations.

The department grants them pay and allowances while undergoing re-training.

Is the department doing anything towards the education of a number of these men in agriculture; and, if so, what buildings are being used for the purpose in connection with some of the agricultural colleges and experimental farms?

Generally speaking, so far as training in agriculture is concerned for men who wish to engage in farming, that is under the Soldiers' Settle-bp.m. ment Board. The Department of Soldiers Re-Establishment do a certain amount of retraining of disabled men who were formerly general farmers. These men are trained in specific branches of farpiing pursuits such as market gardening, poultry raising, operation of tractors, gas engines and farm machinery. It is only to that extent that they provide training in agricultural matters.

I understand that in addition to those men who are partially or totally disabled, there is a class now being educated composed of young men who went overseas when under eighteen years of age. Has the minister ever considered extending -that class to include young students over eighteen who on their return at the age of twenty-two or twenty-three are unable to carry on without some help? They are very desirous of continuing their educational studies. While over eighteen and not suffering from any disability, yet they are unable to go on with their studies for various reasons. I think those men should have consideration.

With reference to those men who enlisted under military age, the Government has decided that some provision should be made for their re-training regardless of whether they have suffered disability or - not. That was discussed in the House earlier in the session. I am sure that decision will be sustained by the judgment of the House and of the country: that the boys who were under eighteen years of age at the time of their enlistment, and who were under no compulsion to go overseas, but voluntarily left to serve their country, should be afforded an opportunity of completing their studies.

Why should a boy of twenty not get the same accommodation when ^he comes back as the boy under eighteen? The boy under eighteen at the time of enlistment has a better, chance than

the boy oi twenty-one, because when the latter comes back it will take him longer to finish his course. The boy under eighteen is discommoded less than the boy under twenty-one who left his studies and voluntarily enlisted.

The man who enlisted when seventeen years of age in the early days of the war is now going on. to twenty-two. He has been away from Canada during the period when, if he were here, he would have proceeded with his education or would have learned a trade. He comes back to Canada at the age of twenty-one or twenty-two without a trade and with his education unfinished, and it has been represented to the Government, and strongly urged in the House, that if some provision be not made for those boys they would drift into the class of common labourers. Those boys were not under obligation to render military service, but they volunteered and went overseas. Therefore the Government decided to deal with those under eighteen years of age. So far the Government has not seen its way clear to help those over eighteen years of age.

Exactly the same argument would apply, so far as I can see, to students over eighteen and under nineteen. They were under no obligation to go overseas, and, as the 'member for Oxford North well said, they are suffering greater disability than boys of sixteen or seventeen. They now come back men, and many of them are desirous of going on with their studies if they can get help. I understand that the Government was considering the education of men who were two years in the university, leaving out matriculants, for whom no provision is made in any way.

The only argument the
minister advances in favour of the idea that boys under eighteen should be considered is that they did not have to go. Well, others who were over eighteen-nineteen and twenty-did not have to go; they enlisted before the Conscription Bill was passed. But the soldier who comes back twenty-five or twenty-six years of age is at a greater disadvantage than the one who comes back under twenty-two.

I think.a distinction should be made between the boy under eighteen who volunteered, say, a year before the war ended, and gave only one year's service, and the boy who enlisted in the early days of the war and gave four or five years' service.

All that has been decided so far is that some provision should be made for all those who enlisted under eighteen years of age; the extent of that provision or the manner of its administration have not yet been settled. The point that my hon. friend makes, however, can be considered when the regulations are being worked out.

I suggest that the age in respect of which this provision is to be made be extended from eighteen to twenty. I know the case o:f a young man nineteen years of age who had been preparing for the matriculation examination. He enlisted and recently returned after having been overseas three and a half years. When the matter is being dealt with I hope that this suggestion will be considered.

The moment you endeavour to divide men up into classes you get on dangerous ground. The case of six young men who enlisted has come under my personal observation. Two of them, under eighteen years of age, enlisted practically as school boys. One was nineteen just starting at the university, and the other three who were from twenty-one to twenty-four years Of age, had completed their education and established themselves in business. Those who had finished their education and had put everything they had in the world into their business felt the call, gave up everything and went to the war; they come back' twenty-six, twenty-seven or twenty-eight years of age and have to make an entirely new start. The boy who was sixteen or seventeen when he enlisted has the advantage of years over these men, and if you compensate the soldier only if he was a certain age when he enlisted, you will get into endless difficulties. It is not practicable to make a dividing line; if you do, there will he overlapping and consequent dissatisfaction. If the department will confine its energies in this regard to the education of men who come back disabled or are unable to provide for themselves, they will be on much safer ground.

Some time ago the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) inquired of the Government whether it was true that the late Gustave Stuart, K.C., of Quebec, had bequeathed his beautiful estate to the country for the purpose of establishing thereon a soldiers' home or a sanatorium. To that question the Secretary of State answered " No " and the Department of Militia " Yes." We have been trying to



find out whether the department, or whatever department the matter may come under, has taken any steps to do something with that property, which is very valuable and surely ought to be taken advantage of.

It is correct that that beautiful property was presented to the Government. It is now being put into shape by this department for the re-training of ex-members of the forces in certain phases of agriculture.

I asked a question early in the session with regard to this matter, and the answer of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment was to the effect that plans were being prepared for the utilization of the property. We have been spending thousands of dollars all over the country in the purchase of properties for the establishment of sanitaria, agricultural farms, and so on. But here is a property, the best located in that part of Quebec, which has been in the possession of the Government for a considerable time; and we are now told that preparations are being made for its use in the re-training of soldiers in some "phases" of .agriculture. May I ask in what phases of agriculture? In what way is the department going to use it, and why was it not used before?
Mr. ROWELL.: At the time it was given the only use the department had for it was to turn it into a hospital, but it was not considered desirable or in the public interest that that should be done at that time, not only because of the character of the place, but because of its situation. There were not the necessary transportation facilities to reach it conveniently, and the necessary water supply for hospital purposes was not available. A considerable expenditure of money would have been necessary to provide an adequate water supply. But the property is well suited for the purpose to which it is now being devoted. I understand that some thirty-five soldiers will shortly be there receiving training in poultry farming, truck gardening, dairying, and activities of that kind in which the soldier who is more or less disabled can engage with advantage to himself and country.

Is it the intention of the Government only to train soldiers in poultry raising or truck gardening on that or any other farm, or will financial arrangements be made to enable returned soldiers to purchase small lots of land in the vicinity of cities for the purpose of carrying on such work?

That is a matter which comes under the Soldier Settlement Board. A Bill is now before the House to deal with that and other aspects of the matter. I do not know its express terms, but, generally speaking, the Government is making provision under that Bill to assist returned soldiers to acquire property for the carrying on of agricultural pursuits.
When, the Bill comes up, the whole matter of its scope and the character of the property to be purchased may be discussed.

I should not like the minister to be under the impression, that water cannot be obtained on the St. Louis road property. It is next the yards occupied by the Transcontinental railway and Government locomotives go there for water many times a year. In the same parish in which this is situated, a tuberculosis hospital has just been, erected by private subscription. and water has also been obtained there. If private citizens have been able to secure water for a private hospital, surely the Government can afford to go to the expense of obtaining water on property which has been granted to them gratuitously.
Maintenance of patients, $3,000,000.

At present 7,800 patients are in the hospitals of the department, 1,800 are being treated in specially designed and equipped sanatoria for the treatment of tuberculosis, 600 suffering from mental disabilities are under the care of specialists in the treatment of mental diseases, 5,400 are receiving intermittent general treatment.
The purchases for this equipment, medicine, food, knd all that is required for maintenance are, of course, made in large quantities. Are tenders called for?
The purchases are made through the War Purchasing Commission.
Are any patients being treated at the Kent House, near Quebec city, or will there be any in the near future?
The Kent House does not come under the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and I .cannot give my hon. friend any information in regard to it.

With reference to the minister's statement that the War Purchasing Commission does the purchasing, is there not a purchasing agent in the Department of Militia, and has he nothing to do with the purchases of these supplies?

The Department of Militia has nothing whatever to do with the purchase of supplies for the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment makes its requisition for the supplies it requires, and the purchases are made under direction of the War Purchasing Commission which supervises everything that is purchased.
Is the minister using existing technical schools in Canada for vocational training, or is he establishing new ones in the different centres? What, for example, is he doing at Halifax?

For the Military District of which Halifax is the centre, the department has three schools of its own for vocational training, but under arrangements it has with fifteen other schools in Nova Scotia, returned soldiers are being trained in those schools. The bulk of the department's work, so far as it relates to vocational training, is (being carried out under an arrangement between the department* and the various institutions existent in Nova Scotia.
Who is in charge?
Professor F. H. Sexton, an officer of the department ds in charge of vocational training, is in charge at Halifax.
The minister said that there were in the province other places where technical education was given to soldiers. What are the names?

I have not the names of the different localities in Nova Scotia, but I shall be glad to get the information, and I will write my hon. friend giving him all the different places where these are in the province.
Mr. LEM'IEUX: Supposing a soldier at Ste. Anne de Bellevue hospital near Montreal wants to get some technical training. If he does not find at the hospital the necessary equipment, is the department doing anything toward sending him, say to the technical schools we have in Montreal?

Yes. A certain phase of this re-training is carried on in the hospital, if the soldier is able to do this work, and it aids in the cure of the patient to have him encouraged to undertake certain work in the hospital. As soon as he is able to be transported from the hospital and to undertake work in an institution or commercial enterprise outside of the hospital, arrangements for that are made.

How many tubercular patients are being treated in sanatoria at the present time, and how many beds has the department ready for returning tubercular soldiers?

There are at present approximately 1,800 tubercular patients undergoing treatment, and approximately 150 vacant beds, so that the hospital accommodation for tubercular patients is at the present time in round figures 1,950 beds. Then, in (those various units which I have mentioned, which are now in course of construction, provision will be made for about 859 additional beds, making a total of about 2,800 beds available for treatment of tubercular patients when the present accommodation is completed.

I am not quite clear as to the scheme under which this department is operating; that is to say, I understood from the minister that a returned soldier, discharged to civilian life, was, if requiring treatment, entitled to free treatment for one year. s Is that correct?

Yes. There are two
classes of cases. A man who is discharged without disability, and who suffers from any disease or injury during a year after discharge gets free treatment if the disability is not due to vice or misconduct. That is a provision made by the Government for the returned soldier, and it is effective for one year after discharge.
That is if he breaks down within a year.

Yes, if he suffers from any disability or disease not due to vice or misconduct. That provision was made a few months ago. If a man breaks down and his collapse is due to or aggravated by service he receives not only free treatment, but pay and allowances for himself and his actual dependents so long as he is thus disabled.
I understand there is a soldiers' home in Ottawa; what does it cost per day per patient?
I do not know to what home my hon. friend refers.
The Soldiers' Home in the city of Ottawa.

There is no Soldiers' Home in Ottawa operated by this department. There may ,be an hospital under the Department of Militia and Defence. I believe there is the Sir 'Sanford Fleming Home, but I have no knowledge of that.

Vocational Expense, Administration and Training, $750,000.
What does that include?

This includes the administration and training in the vocational branch. It covers such matters as maintenance, repairs, light, heat, and power, stationery and office supplies, ear fares of soldiers attending classes, telephones, telegrams, laundry and clothing expenses, subsistence of staff, subsistence of students attending vocational school. That would be the meals they might have there while the school was in session.

Has any part of this
amount been expended?
Mr. ROWEILiL: No; this is a vote for the present year. The actual expenditure last year on this head was $645,452. The amount is larger this year because there will be a larger number of students attending these vocational classes..

This is a very
large item for salaries, and it does not include all salaries, because doctors and nurses are under a separate item. Cooks, orderlies and general staff are also separate. It seems that a very large proportion of the whole expenditure is salaries, and it 'would be well to have some explanation of this item.

Previous to the transfer to the Department of Militia and Defence of a number of hospitals operated by the Military Hospitals Commission, men who broke down as a result of their war service were given treatment in hospitals by the Military Hospitals Commission, and their pay and allowances were issued by the Department of Militia and Defence. Do I understand the minister to say that we have 7,381 employees in this branch?

our. The personnel served by the department has increased three-fold during the past year and probably the peak of the load has not yet been reached.
May I interrupt the minister to ask what connection this has with the Department of Labour?

Before I answer the hon. member there are two or three facts I would like to give the Committee. This salary item varies, as pray be supposed, with the general variation in the number of men cared for. The occupational work carried on in hospitals by this branch has been developed considerably during the past year. On April 1, 1918, the number of men undergoing curative training, together with those in attendance in certain work shops, was 3,817, while on April 1, 1919, the number was 9,059, thus entailing increased instructional facilities together with increased cost of administration. It is expected that the rate of growth will be materially accelerated in the near future. For the last three months the increase has been at the rate of about 2,000 per month. My hon. friend has asked what is the relation of this work to the Department of Labour? Under the Act passed last session whereby provision is made for co-operation between the Federal Department of Labour and various Provincial Governments, a number of employment offices have been established throughout Canada. In each of these offices there is a representative of the Department of Soldiers' 'Civil Re-Establishment. That representative is paid out of this vote. The object of having a representative of the department in each of these employment offices is to ensure that the returned soldier when he comes seeking employment not only gets a fair show, but is given the preference as far as is possible. It is proving to be of great advantage to have representatives of the department in all these employment offices throughout Canada. The representative is there to meet the soldier when he comes in, and to keep track of all opportunities of employment that may be available and to acquaint the men of them. I am glad to say that the results are proving very gratifying.
Up to the 17th of May, just a week ago, the number of applications from demobilized soldiers for employment was 30,146. The total number placed in positions was 22,838, being 75.7 per cent of the number of applications received. In addition to the placing of demobilized soldiers in employment.

the representatives of this branch have interviewed on their return to Canada 150,297 members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force with a view to giving them information or assistance, and particularly for the purpose of properly informing each man as to the benefits which are provided by the Government of Canada for him.
The number of men seeking information from the representatives of the department on matters other than placement in employment averages about 40,000 per month.
Under this branch information was gathered from every soldier on the field as to the particular occupation or pursuit in which he would like to engage on his return.
The department has information collected from all the soldiers who were overseas which gives a full record in the case of every soldier and the occupation in which he desires to engage on his return to Canada. This involved the collection and tabulation of over 6,000,000 items of information. We were able to ascertain what percentage of men desired to engage in any particular occupation. All that information was collected and tabulated by the Information and Service Branch of the Department.
Does that include university training on the other side?
No; the Khaki University is under the Department of Militia and Defence.
I would like more details from the minister about this large item of -$5,178,420. What is it for?
Salaries-Administrative, clerical and indus-'trial re-training.
Will the minister tell me how large a staff he has in these different branches?

The total number of employees to be paid out of this vote, on the 31st March, 1919, was 3,891. Of these 37.8 per cent are females in clerical positions not sought by returned soldiers. Of the total remaining 34.8 per cent had seen service in France; 4.7 per cent had seen service in England; 4.2 per cent had seen service in Canada; 2.2 per cent had been rejected or exempted; 6.6 per cent were over age or under age, and only 6.4 per cent were male employees who had not seen service in the C.E.F.
You are classifying them altogether?
That is classifying them altogether.

1,698 actually served with the forces or 43.7 per cent of the total number of staff. If females are excluded the percentage of those who served with the forces is 81.5 per cent.

to express the wish that the minister who is piloting these Estimates through the House would impress upon the minister in charge of this department the necessity of giving greater consideration to the claims of returned soldiers. With regard to these many items of information which have been furnished, could the minister tell me how *many times the overseas soldiers were examined in order to secure these 6,000,000 items? The department has a system of follow-up in all oases where em-

ployment is secured with a view to seeing if the employment. is satisfactory and assisting the soldiers in finding permanent positions. I know a farmer, a returned soldier, who went to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment looking for a position. It was in winter, and he could not farm then. He was offered a position as chauffeur for a doctor. " That is the only position we have," they said, " take it or leave it." The transfer has not been made yet?

The minister this afternoon announced that he was going to establish that service. I have every reason to believe that the Canadian Army Dental Corps is to be continued for service to the Militia Department, and that this new branch is to be used in the service of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment.

I think my hon. friend understood me, but perhaps some other hon. members did not. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is not taking over the Dental Corps, but is establishing a branch for treating the ex-members of the forces coming under its care.
Major-General MEWBURN: We felt that during demobilization we could not disband the dental service. A very large number of men are coming back from overseas or are here already, some thirty thousand, who will require further dental treatment. Many of them are suffering from trench mouth and other mouth diseases, and it would be manifestly unfair not to give them treatment. At first we thought it could be done in connection with the Department of Soldiers' Civil. Re-Establishment, but that was not considered feasible. So after consultation, we decided to continue the Dental Service during the period of demobilization, so that the men requiring treatment could get it.

I approve most thoroughly of the course which is being followed by both departments in connection with the dental service. In the position I occupied in Military District No. 12, it was my duty and opportunity to observe conditions, and I know something of them. Many of the men are coming back from overseas in a most deplorable condition, dentally speaking. The conditions under which they have been living for the last two or three years have brought about a dental condition which is very very difficult to deal with to-day, and the minister is absolutely right when he says that they should receive the necessary dental treatment until they are at least in the condition in which they were when they enlisted. It will take a considerable time, some months, for the Dental Corps as now established to finish up their work in connection with the Militia Department. It cannot be done in the time which was first specified, namely, sixty days after discharge; that is absolutely impossible. It would nave been equally impossible, if the corps had been demobilized as at first proposed, to attend to these men in our hospitals because they are already occupied by patients who require quietness more or less. Further, it would be utterly impossible for as satisfactory a service to be given in the hospitals, because the treatment is entirely different from that of the Dental Corps. For these reasons it was found advisable not to demobilize the corps, and I approve as strongly as I can of the course which is being pursued. I am satisfied that in about a year-I hope less- it will be possible to demobilize the corps, but I believe it will be necessary to continue for a very much longer period of time a Dental Service in connection with the hospitals..

In my own town I know a young man who lost his sight, and after coming iback from France he entered some school of vocational training in England-II forget its name.
Would itbe St. Dunstan's?

I think so. First he learned stenography and became an efficient stenographer-and I mention it as an extraordinary thing that a man totally blind could learn stenography-but he was a strong, active fellow and preferred manual work, so in the same college he took up a carpentry course, which he completed. On returning home the college authorities gave him two suits of clothes and $250 cash. I do not know what the arrangement is, but I thought it was a very excellent institution, and if we have more of such institutions we will be doing some good.

An arrangement was
worked out between the department and St. Dunstan's Hostel in England for the training of blinded ex-members of the Canadian Forces. Further arrangements have now been made for the continuation of their training if necessary in Canadian institutions. The St. Dunstan's scheme of aftercare for the blind is being fostered in Canada from Pearson Hall at Toronto, called after Sir Arthur Pearson, the head of St. Dunstan s Hostel. What they have done for the blind is almost a miracle, and too great credit cannot be given to Sir Arthur Pearson. We are trying to follow his example here.

This is a very important .matter affecting a question of the highest importance and one in which the Dominion Government ought to have been represented.

On the motion of Mr. J. M. Douglas for the return to the Senate of the evidence taken in divorce cases:

I am informed that the fees in these divorce cases are remitted. Of course in doing this we are facilitating the granting of divorces by the Parliament of Canada. I do not sit in the Committee when these cases come up because I do not recognize divorce, but as a public man and as a Canadian, I am appalled at the number of divorces Parliament is granting. There are more divorces during this session than since 'Confederation and that is a period of half a century. I had always thought that Canada was a British country, but we are being fast Americanized: In the United States there is one divorce for every twelve marriages. Ottawa is becoming the Reno of Canada as a result of the granting of innumerable divorces. I take the number of divorce Bills that we have passed this evening. Ten have received their third reading and five or six their second reading. Going on at this rate, it is evident that we are passing through a social revolution. The institution of the family on which sqciety rests is passing through a crucial test indeed. I would certainly object to the remission of the fees in these cases.
Motion agreed to.

Arisaig-repairs to wharf, $3,000.
['That the resolution be considered item by item.']

When will that
work be done?
Hon. F. B. CARVELL (Minister of Public
Works): We will proceed with it just as soon as the money is available. Wherever it is possible, to prepare the plans and specifications they are being prepared and there will be some cases in connection with this list in which we have actually called for tenders before the money is voted, taking the ground that a vote of one-sixth of the Estimates is a justification for proceeding. We have found in the past, and I believe it has been the experience of all ministers and of the department generally that a great deal of time is lost by reason of waiting until the Estimates are all passed by the House. It takes some time to get these works under way and our intention is to have the work started at the earliest possible moment and to have it finished before cold weather comes on.

This work is very much needed. The wharf at Arisaig is in very bad condition. But if the Department of Public Works comes along in its usual leisurely way, I am afraid the work will be of very little use to the people during the present season. I would urge upon the minister the importance of having this matter attended to with as little delay as possible.

I appreciate that.
Boisdale-wharf, $1,800.

That is to replace a
wharf that was there -before?
Yes, for repairs.

Does the minister intend calling for tenders?
[iMr. Lemieux.]

Yes.
East Bay Beach-wharf extension, $650.
Is that the wharf at the head of the bay?
Beach Bay is off the Bras d'Or lake somewhere. My hon. friend ought to know the geography of it.

I know the place very well. It used to be called the Head of the Bay.
Ecum Secum-completion of wharf, $1,700. Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR: What is meant by "completion?" That wharf was built not - more than eight or ten years ago. I understand it is not in very good repair, and that this money is being voted for the purpose of putting the wharf in repair. Am I right in that?

This is for the building up of a crib 40 by 40 feet and 4 feet high, and also the building up of a crib 26 by 20 feet and 10 feet high, in order to complete the wharf which was constructed in 1914.
Gabarus-extension of beach protection, $1000.
Is that for a new work or is it to extend a section of Gabarus harbour?
This is to continue the pile protection work to the already existing wharf and for the protection of the harbour.

Last fall, or a year ago last fall, there was a terrific gale that did a great deal of damage to public works in that district. Many claims or demand^ came to the department for repairs after the storm. I understand that there was considerable damage done to the wharf at Gabarus. This is probably for replacing or extending the work that was done before?

It is.
I-iivingstone's Cove-to repair and strengthen wharf, $4,600.

What is to be
done there?

This is to repair the
damage caused by the severe storm of November, 1918. A cribwork block 65 feet long, 16 feet wide, and of an average depth of 16 feet, is to be constructed. The block will have a creosoted substructure.
What I said about Arisaig applies to these other places.

I can assure my hon.
friend it applies to every public work for which I am asking an appropriation. I appreciate as much as anybody the necessity of getting to work early. I admit that we did not make as early a start last year as we should have done, and I am afraid that in many cases this year we shall not accomplish all we wish to do. Every week I demand from the engineering office a statement of the entire progress on all important works under the department; a statement also of the works for which tenders are being called; a statement of the works in respect of which we shall be able to call for tenders next week; and another statement showing the preparations. I find that demanding this information hurries things along. We must have about three or four dozen works now actually contracted for in different parts of the country for which the money has not yet actually been voted.
Has the material been ordered for the work at Livingstone's Cove, and have any steps been taken in- the construction of the wharf?

No. The difficulty is this: We are taking the ground that on any public work for which we can call for tenders we are justified in calling for tenders even before the Main Estimates are voted, but in respect of works which must be done by day labour, such as small repairs like this, we have to have the money voted before we can pay the bills.

We voted one-sixth part of the Estimates some two months ago. That would surely enable the minister to take some action in preparing for the work this summer. At least, he could have contracted for the material. 1 presume that in nearly all these cases the work will have to be done by day labour because you cannot very well contract for these repairs. Consequently, it is of the greatest importance that material should be ordered as early in the season as possible. This is one of the worst seasons of the year in which to obtain material in that locality, because the farmers are all busy and no one can be got to do that kind of work, whereas a month or two ago they would have -been very glad of the opportunity of taking out some timber and getting ready for the season's work. But that time has passed, and there is no help for it. All I will say is that it is not the way we would like the business to be done. There is very urgent need of the repairs to Malignant Cove, which is the next item, and the deputy minister was kind enough to tell me that he would do something towards having those repairs made. The top of the wharf has been carried off and landed in a field some distance away, where some farmer rescued it. The planks are there and it is very important that the repairs should be made because a ship discharges there and the wharf is required for the goods. Has the minister had any word from the locality about what is being done there?

No, T dp not think any word has come back. But positive instructions were given to the engineer to proceed with the work at once. As to the other wharf my hon. friend referred to, I cannot say that instructions have been given to procure materials for this particular work, but we have already made arrangements for a large amount of material in all parts of Canada in order to be ready to start work as soon as the money is available.
Neil's Harbour-repairs to breakwater wharf,

This wharf is also a breakwater. Neil's Harbour is a fishing village of considerable importance, and before the breakwater was constructed the fishermen did not have very much shelter for their boats, and consequently had to haul their boats up every night and launch them next morning. Since the breakwater was constructed they have been able to anchor inside, and this convenience has brought quite a number of new settlers to Neil's Harbour. In the terrific storm last year the breakwater was- pretty badly battered, and I presume the minister has received a report on the damage done.

The damage was caused in the terrific gale of November 4, 1918. The estimated cost of the repairs is $1,100, covering round timber, guard rails, face-timbers, sheathing, covering, fenders, ballast, etc.

I hope that $1,100 will be enough to restore the breakwater to its former condition. But as soon as possible the minister should have the breakwater extended for about its present length. The shelter afforded by -the present breakwater is not very great, and on account of the number of 'boats-and larger boats are coming there for shelter-there is not sufficient space for all behind the breakwater, and the request of t-he fishermen for some years back has been that the breakwater should be extended so as to give them more room. I can assure the minister that it is not

throwing money away to increase the fishing facilities along the coast of Nova Scotia. It is quite unnecessary to point out what a splendid food is the fish these fishermen catch, and how important it is they should have the opportunity of taking this harvest of the sea where there is an abundance of [DOT] it; but it is impossible to reap the harvest unless, facilities of this kind are put at the disposal of the fishermen. I keenly realize that money is scarce and hard to get-I must say, however, that large votes are being taken which I think could have been postponed for the present-and in view of the financial condition of the country I have not the appetite, shall I say, to press very hard for an expenditure at the present moment, but I trust that when our finances are in a little better shape this breakwater will be extended.
I would like the minister to bear in mind that we had in the Estimates of 1911-12 large votes for works in various parts of the Dominion-considerable of which was in the county that I represent. The Minister of Public Works of that time, Hon. Mr. Rogers, always told us that as soon as the war was over and conditions got better the works so provided for would be the first to receive the attention of the Government. Carrying out that idea, if the minister will look back to what was in the Estimates in 1911-12 after the change of Government, he will see that a great-many of the works -have been dropped.
I cannot put my finger on the page of Hansard where that promise was made, but it was made repeatedly, that before the Government undertook anything new in the line of public works the old programme would be carried out. If the old programme were carried out in regard to my own county I would be very well satisfied, for facilities would be afforded to the fishermen along the eastern coast of the counties of Victoria and Cape Breton that would be of very great benefit indeed. And those facilities would not be altogether for the benefit of the local fishermen. Boats come from all parts of Nova Scotia to the fishing grounds off the coast, and safe anchorage is just as necessary for them as for the local boats. I have said on several occasions, and I repeat it now, that no other industry in Canada to-day holds out such prospect of profitable development as the fisheries both of the Atlantic and the Pacific coast, and I would impress upon the minister and the Government the opportunity which presents itself to them to make a record in connection with the de-

velopment and proper handling of that great industry.
Port Hood-wharf repairs and extension, ? 7,000.

What repairs were
done at Port Hood?
This is to repair the present work and to construct a new block 20 by 100 feet. on the southern end of the block constructed during 1914-15. It is estimated that the cost will be $7,000.

This wharf has an exposed location which renders it essential that the work should be done as soon as possible. As to the importance of the wharf I need say nothing, for it is the only wharf along that shore, and quite a trade is carried on there. Unless the work is done early in the summer it cannot be undertaken at all.

This work will be pushed forward just as rapidly as possible.
Saw Pit-wharf improvements, $1,000.
This is something new. We have heard about a mere sawdust wharf; this is Saw Pit wharf?
It is in Lunenburg county, but it is not a sawdust wharf.
There are two Saw Pit wharves in Nova Scotia. 'I am not sure if this is in Lunenburg county or not-I hope it is.

This is in Lunenburg county. It is only worth $1,000. It might be built partly of sawdust-I am not sure.
Scotch Cove (White Point)-breakwater extension, $8,400.
There is a White Point in my county, but I do not think this is my White Point.
It is in Queens county, I hope.

No, it is in North Cape Breton. It is for the purpose of extending the present breakwater. The contract is for an extension, 50 feet long by
9 p.m. 30 feet wide, to the present breakwater which was originally built at a cost of $28,934.

This extension is just exactly the improvement that I was praying for at Neil's Harbour, but we have reason to be thankful that we are getting this extension. White Point would be a better name for the place than Scotch Cbve. It may be called Scotch Cove, but not to

my knowledge. I think when the wharf was built it was called White Point wharf.
Yarmouth Bar-repairs and improvements, $4,500.

I have directed the
attention of the department to the need of repairs to the wharf at Baddeck. There are breaks in the sides and at the ends; the ballast is running out, and the condition of the wharf is getting bad very rapidly. There is much tourist travel at that point in the summer season, and we take pride in the good appearance of our wharves and landing-places. The repairs required are not very extensive, and I hope the minister will do what is necessary to put this wharf in good shape.
Mr. C'AJRVELL: That is under consideration.

These Estimates were
prepared, I assume, some months ago, and since their - preparation the minister has no doubt received from his officials information which will be very useful in the preparation of the Supplementary Estimates. I take it for granted that in urgent cases brought to the minister's attention by his own engineers, provision will be made for such works as may be necessary. At all events, we may be permitted to hope so.

If I provided in the
Supplementary Estimates for all works that have been suggested by engineers and interested parties 'the amount would stagger my hon. friend, who for many years was the watch-dog of the Treasury. These small works, which are constructed chiefly of wood, are naturally subject to the wear and tear of the elements, and during the war they have probably not been taken care of as they should have been. A series of storms last autumn caused damage along the Atlantic coast which will probably run into half a million dollars. In many cases we were unable to have accurate surveys made at the time these Estimates were prepared, and my hon. friend is right in saying that we have much information today which we did not have then. I am afraid, therefore, that additional amounts will have to be voted in the Supplementary Estimates in respect of many of the items in the Main Estimates.
'Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR:	A work in my
constituency that is in very much need of attention is the breakwater at New Harbour. This breakwater was built ten or twelve years ago-perhaps more than that -but it was never finished and it is not
sufficiently long to protect all the fishing boats. Before the breakwater was built, the fishermen there had to pull their boats upon the beach and sometimes sit up all night to look after them in case of a storm. After the construction of the breakwater a certain number of boats were able to find shelter behind it, and a flourishing village has grown up at that place, where a large fishing business is carried on. But the breakwater is not long enough to protect all the boats that operate in that harbour; when a storm comes some of them are unable to crowd in behind the breakwater. In 1911 the Government of that day voted $10,000 to complete this breakwater by extending it some 300 feet or more out into the harbour. The vote was carried along for one or two years after the change of Government and then it was dropped, with the promise that it would be restored. But time has passed and nothing has been done. I have not been asking for anything in my constituency during the war, because I wanted to assist the Government in saving as much money as possible. As a matter of fact, there is only one small item in these estimates for the county of Guys-borough. That is for $1,700 for repairs to one wharf. There are 150 miles of coast line in Guysborough county. That county is also one of the greatest fishing counties in Nova Scotia. I wish to say that the case of New Harbour is a very urgent one. I see that $60,000 is appropriated for harbours and rivers generally in Nova Scotia. I do not know whether the minister could find the money in that vote for this work at New Harbour, but I do know that nowhere along the coast of that province is a work more needed than it is at that place. I would urge the minister and his staff to do something in the matter and provide shelter for the fishing boats and greatly assist production in that locality. No expenditure anywhere in Canada has produced better results than have come about through the construction of the breakwater in that harbour, but unless we complete it, sufficient protection for the fishermen who do business there will not be afforded. I leave the matter in the hands of the minister, and would urge him to give it special attention.
Another matter has been drawn to my attention, a very important one, about which nothing has been done. At Wine Harbour, further west on the Atlantic coast, a storm filled up the channel. The boats could not get in or out of the harbour, and the cellars in the village were flooded with water. When the people asked the

Public Works Department to do something about it, they got the reply that the department had nothing to do with it; that it was purely a muncipal affair. But it was the closing of the mouth of the harbour by the storm that caused the trouble in the village. While the department is not responsible for keeping water out of cellars it is part of its duty to keep the harbour open. A very small amount of hand dredging would have done the work. There was no municipal authority to attend to it and it has not been done. I submit, with all seriousness, that it is really the duty of the Public Works Department to open up that harbour with as little delay as possible. Will the minister do it?

I have heard of the
latter case; it was brought to my attention some time ago. I cannot agree with my hon. friend that the Public Works Department was responsible for the storm. My hon. friend might have a logical reason for asking the department to dredge out the sand and gravel that have been deposited by the storm, but I do not think that we can be held responsible for the flooding of cellars. As to the other matter, this is the first 1 have heard of it. Although this work is well known in the department, the particular matter mentioned by my hon. friend has not been brought to my personal attention. I shall be happy to give it the best consideration that I can. I would not like to say that it will be provided for out of the general vote of $60,000; it has been the experience of the department that these general votes are always required to take care of ordinary matters that come up during the year. A storm arises and a wharf or a breakwater is damaged to some extent, and it has to be repaired immediately. But if it be at all possible, I will endeavour to see if we cannot build the extension asked for by my hon. friend.
Harbours and rivers generally-repairs and improvements, $14,000.

Under this item I should like to ask the minister regarding a couple of public works which are very necessary and to which I have already directed his attention. One is the projected boat harbour at North lake, in King's county. The minister has before him all the data concerning this work and is also advised of the reasons why it is so necessary. What a haven it would be for fishing boats along the coa'st, because there is no other place within twenty-five mileS where they can enter for shelter. These are excellent fishing

grounds. Thij public work was projected before the war, and tenders were called for, but in consequence of the outbreak of the war the matter was dropped. Since then nature has done something to our advantage; it has changed the outlet of the lake, and under present conditions it will not require more than about one-third of what it would have originally cost to construct this work. In addition to this, if the harbour is built and solid side walls constructed, it would afford the provincial government an opportunity of building a bridge across the outlet, which would be of great convenience to the people, shortening their travel in that section. I sincerely trust the minister will be able to bring down in his Supplementary Estimates an amount sufficient for this public work so extremely necessary, and which I have been endeavouring to get for the last two or three years.
I have also called the minister's attention to the necessity for a small wharf at a point on a little island called Boughton island, on which there are some eighteen or twenty farmers who are great producers, but who have no means of getting the products of their farms-and they are good farmers-to Prince Edward Island, which for them is the mainland, across a small strait, except in dories. The provincial government have projected a highway right across the centre of the island down to tide-water, and if such a wharf as desired could be built, at which large gasoline boats could be loaded, it would be of the greatest possible convenience to these people who are so isolated, and would enable them to carry their products to the mainland. If the minister would be able to bring down in his Supplementary Estimates amounts to cover these two items of necessary public expenditure it would be deemed a great favour and would be of the greatest possible convenience to the people to be served thereby.

I want to assure the constituents of my hon. friend that, if they do not get these works it will not be because their representative has not done his duty.
Quebec-Gross Isle quarantine station, extension of wharves, $>50,000.
Has a contract been given for this work?

No. The plans are practically completed now and we are about to call for tenders.
Isle Verte-repairs to wharf.

Isle Verte is on the south side, but opposite Isle Verte there is

Green Island, and I regret to -see that there is not a sum sufficient to finish or extend even one work there. The residents of this place are not wealthy. It is very difficult for them !to send their products to Quebec, and the river is their only means of transport. A few years ago they started two wharves, one at the upper and the other at the lower end of the island. The one at the upper end is not completed, and the lower one, opposite Isle Verte, should be extended so as to enable the biggest schooner to reach the wharf. These people exported last year over 24,000 bushels of potatoes to Quebec, and apart from the fish they catch, this is all they have to live on. I should like the minister to take a note of this matter with a view to seeing if there is a possibility of having an extension built on the lower wharf, the cost of which will only be a few hundred dollars.
This is the first time this matter has been brought to my attention as far as I can remember. I shall certainly take a note of the matter and have an investigation made.

I was sorry to see that sufficient work had not been done at Isle Verte, but I must say that I was pleased that nothing had been done at Cacouna East. I would like to know if the report is true that some money is to be expended on the wharf at Cacouna East. I do not want to take up the time of the committee in speaking about that small wharf, but I think it is a useless wharf and an expenditure of money on it will be unnecessary. I understand that $100 is to be spent on it this summer.

I have no personal
knowledge of the matter but will be glad to make an investigation. Only yesterday the hon. gentleman spoke to me about it and I have not had time to consider The subject. The amount is very small, but if as he says it is unnecessary to spend the money the expenditure ought not to be made.

Only two years ago an expenditure was made merely for the purpose of erecting a fence on each side of the approach to the wharf, and if the minister were acquainted with the locality he would know that the money was uselessly spent. The municipal road skirts the shore and the farmers reside south of the road. The road is free and there is no necessity whatever for a fence because there are no cattle
to trespass. It is a very easy matter to have petitions signed. I know that the resident engineer is anxious to convince the minister that the wharf was a necessity, but unfortunately the member wants to impress on the minister that it is not, and that in fact that the wharf is useless. It is a contest between the member and the resident engineer, who, however, by some means or other succeeded in having a petition signed by about a hundred persons. I am told that even merchants six or seven miles down in Isle Verte signed the petition insisting on the necessity of a wharf at Cacouna East. It is all very well to have a hundred signatures to a petition, and I am not opposed to the expenditure of money in my riding when I am convinced that there is a real necessity for it, but when I see $100 spent for nothing, just to please an individual I must enter a protest, and accordingly I call the minister's attention to the matter.

If the faots are as stated by the member the money will not be expended. I will see that an investigation is made immediately.
St. Laurent, Island of Orleans-Repairs to wharf, $15,000.

With regard to the wharf on the Island of Orleans this item is rather large but I suppose it is due to the storm that occurred last fall destroying the wharf. I understand that the policy generally followed by the department is that when an amount is voted exceeding $5,000 the work must be given by contract and tenders called for. But I would urge upon the minister, owing to the wharf having been practically destroyed, the necessity of having the works started at once and not waiting until tenders are called for. The same remark applies to the wharf at St. Jean, wffiich has suffered from the same storm and is in about the same condition.
St. Anne de BeauprS-Wharf repairs and reconstruction, $39,000.

As regards the item under discussion-(Ste. Anne de Beaupre-over a week ago special orders were given for the construction of a temporary landing place with a plank walk leading to the shore and it is our hope that the work will be all completed inside of two weeks from to-day or to-morrow at the outside. We realized that if this work was to be of use this year it must be done immediately because of the immense traffic that takes place there in the month of June. A temporary landing will therefore be ready inside of two weeks

What is this very interesting law point? Is it about land?

The point is whether the seigneurs have the ownership in the sites of all the wharves down the river St. Lawrence which are located upon the seig-neuries. A sort of test case is being raised at Riviere du Loup.
The pretext of the seigneurs is that they are the owners of the land down to low tide, and they claim that you have no right to place the wharf there unless you pay a certain amount to them.
That we are practically trespassers in very many cases.

I am surprised that that point has not been settled. When I was Solicitor General the case came before the department. The Seigneur of Riviere du Loup claimed that he was the sole proprietor of the seaweed.- People from time immemorial had gathered the seaweed in summer time but he claimed that, under his title, the people could not take the seaweed. I had a commission appointed by the Department of Marine and Fisheries and, if I remember correctly, the commission decided that it was not a weed, but an animal; it even had claws, and therefore the seigneur, Mr. Fraser, could not claim to be entitled to the seaweed. That was the decision given by Professor Prince after consultation with another authority on fish. It would be a very easy thing for the department to determine whether the seigneur can claim the shore as his property; his rights must be well defined in the title. We had a similar case in Gaspe around Grande River. We had the ease tested, and the preposterous claims of the seignieur were set aside by the Privy Council, and the people were given the right to use the shore.

The case is not the same in all the seigneuries. In the case at
177J
Riviere du Loup the title given by the King of France was to certain land along the river St. Lawrence with the shore and shelter in front of that land. In other seigneuries, title is given only as far as the river, and does not include the shore. I do not think the seigneurs have any right to claim compensation for the land on which a wharf i3 built, because in all the titles navigation rights are excepted. Of course, wharves are built for navigation purposes, and surely the rights of the public are paramount to those of the seigneurs. I do not think the Government would have any difficulty in winning these cases.

That is the point at issue. I have not studied it closely, but I know generally what the situation is. The case is under preparation by the department to be tested out in the courts, and when the case is decided we shall know what the court says, at all events. I am afraid the decision of Professor Prince is not of very much assistance to us when a wharf is in question, because while a wharf may have claws to fasten it to the ground, it could hardly be construed as an animal.

With regard to this item, perhaps the minister may think that we are quite persistent in our request for certain works on the River St. Charles, in the province of Quebec. The sewage of at least three-quarters of the city of Quebec enters into the St. Charles river above the location of this dam and before the work was started an agreement was made with the city of Quebec by which they were to provide for the sewage.

would very much like to go on with ihis work. In July last I had some correspondence with the mayor of Quebec.
